claim: Existing genetic methods of neuronal targeting do not routinely achieve the resolution required for mapping brain circuits.
source: Existing genetic methods of neuronal targeting do not routinely achieve the resolution required for mapping brain circuits.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that frames the motivation for the work, representing an assessment of the current state of the field.

claim: The SpaRCLIn method relies on first isolating neurons within a targeted group according to their developmental lineages.
source: The method relies on first isolating neurons within a targeted group (i.e. Gal4 pattern) according to their developmental lineages
evidence: This describes the first step of the SpaRCLIn methodology as presented in the abstract.

claim: The SpaRCLIn method intersectionally limits the number of lineages by selecting only those in which two distinct neuroblast enhancers are active.
source: and then intersectionally limiting the number of lineages by selecting only those in which two distinct neuroblast enhancers are active.
evidence: This describes the second step of the SpaRCLIn methodology as presented in the abstract.

claim: The neuroblast enhancers drive expression of split Cre recombinase fragments.
source: The neuroblast enhancers drive expression of split Cre recombinase fragments.
evidence: This describes a key component of the SpaRCLIn system as stated in the abstract.

claim: Split Cre fragments are fused to non-interacting pairs of split inteins.
source: These are fused to non-interacting pairs of split inteins
evidence: This describes the molecular design of the split Cre components in the SpaRCLIn system.

claim: Non-interacting pairs of split inteins ensure reconstitution of active Cre when all fragments are expressed in the same neuroblast.
source: which ensure reconstitution of active Cre when all fragments are expressed in the same neuroblast.
evidence: This describes the function of split inteins in the SpaRCLIn system as stated in the abstract.

claim: Active Cre renders all neuroblast-derived cells in a lineage permissive for Gal4 activity.
source: Active Cre renders all neuroblast-derived cells in a lineage permissive for Gal4 activity.
evidence: This describes the mechanism by which Cre activity enables Gal4 function in the SpaRCLIn system.

claim: The SpaRCLIn system can facilitate neural circuit-mapping in Drosophila.
source: We demonstrate how this system can facilitate neural circuit-mapping in Drosophila.
evidence: This is a summary claim from the abstract about the utility of the system, supported by the examples provided in the manuscript.

claim: It has proved relatively easy to target large groups of neurons using binary expression systems in genetic model organisms.
source: While it has proved relatively easy to target large groups of neurons for cellular manipulation by this means in genetic model organisms using binary expression systems, such as the Cre-lox system of mice or the Gal4-UAS system of fruit flies
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of genetic targeting methods, drawing on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Highly-specific targeting of neurons requires combinatorial methods.
source: highly-specific targeting of neurons requires combinatorial methods.
evidence: This is a statement about the requirements for achieving specific neuronal targeting, based on established knowledge.

claim: Genetic combinatorial methods typically use either the regulatory elements of two neurally-expressed genes or exploit stochastic events to limit transgene targeting.
source: Genetic combinatorial methods typically use either the regulatory elements of two neurally-expressed genes or exploit stochastic events to limit transgene targeting to a subpopulation of a larger group of neurons.
evidence: This describes the two main types of combinatorial genetic methods used in the field.

claim: Both types of combinatorial methods have been used to target single cells under optimal conditions in fruit flies.
source: In fruit flies, both types of method have been used to target single cells under optimal conditions (Aso et al., 2014; Gao et al., 2008; Gordon and Scott, 2009; Kohatsu et al., 2011; Lee and Luo, 1999; Luan et al., 2012; Pool et al., 2014; Sen et al., 2019; Shang et al., 2008; Yu et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published work demonstrating single-cell targeting.

claim: Combinatorial approaches using three regulatory elements have achieved some success in fruit flies.
source: and combinatorial approaches using three regulatory elements have achieved some success (Dolan et al., 2017; Pankova and Borst, 2017; Shirangi et al., 2016; Sullivan et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work using three-element combinatorial approaches.

claim: Stochastic methods are poorly reproducible by nature.
source: stochastic methods are, by nature, poorly reproducible
evidence: This is a logical inference about the inherent properties of stochastic methods.

claim: Combinatorial methods are labor-intensive, often requiring the characterization of many neurally active enhancer elements.
source: while combinatorial methods are labor-intensive, often requiring the characterization of many neurally active enhancer elements (Dionne et al., 2018; Tirian et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim about the labor-intensive nature of combinatorial methods is supported by citations.

claim: Simpler methods of targeting small populations of brain cells are desirable in the effort to comprehensively map neural function.
source: Simpler methods of targeting small populations of brain cells are therefore desirable in the effort to comprehensively map neural function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the limitations of existing methods, representing an inference about what is needed.

claim: An attractive approach to increase the specificity of neuronal targeting is to identify neurons based on both their terminal gene expression and their developmental history.
source: An attractive approach to increase the specificity of neuronal targeting is to identify neurons based not only on the genes they express in the terminally differentiated state (i.e. terminal effector genes, TEG), but also on their developmental history (Awasaki et al., 2014; Dymecki et al., 2010; Huang, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to work that has explored this approach.

claim: Most neuronal lineages produce diverse neuron types.
source: Most neuronal lineages produce diverse neuron types
evidence: This is a statement about the general properties of neuronal lineages, based on established knowledge.

claim: Lineage identity, in general, correlates poorly with neuronal identity as defined by gene expression.
source: and while some striking correspondences have been found (Lacin et al., 2019), lineage identity, in general, correlates poorly with neuronal identity as defined by gene expression (Hobert et al., 2016; Zeng and Sanes, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work on the relationship between lineage and gene expression.

claim: Gene expression is often correlated across neurons that differ in identity as defined by their function, morphology, and neuroanatomical location.
source: Conversely, gene expression is often correlated across neurons that differ in identity as defined by their function, morphology, and neuroanatomical location (Hobert, 2016; Hobert and Kratsios, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work on gene expression patterns in neurons.

claim: Neuronal identities are defined by the expression of often overlapping batteries of terminal effector genes, not by single genes.
source: This is because neuronal identities are defined not by single genes, but by the expression of often overlapping batteries of TEGs.
evidence: This is an inference about how neuronal identity is determined, based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: An intersection of lineage with the expression of a specific terminal effector gene may include fewer neurons than an intersection of the expression patterns of two terminal effector genes.
source: An intersection of lineage with the expression of a specific TEG may thus, in general, include fewer neurons than an intersection of the expression patterns of two TEGs.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the potential advantages of lineage-based intersections.

claim: Neurons from a given lineage typically remain regionally localized.
source: In addition, because neurons from a given lineage typically remain regionally localized
evidence: This is a statement about the spatial properties of neuronal lineages, based on established knowledge.

claim: Intersections made using lineage information will tend to restrict neuronal targeting anatomically.
source: intersections made using lineage information will tend to restrict neuronal targeting anatomically.
evidence: This is an inference about the consequences of using lineage information for targeting.

claim: Recombinase-based intersectional methods that combine information about lineage and cell type have been developed in both mice and fruit flies.
source: Recombinase-based intersectional methods that combine information about lineage and cell type have been developed in both mice and fruit flies and have been shown to substantially restrict targeting to cell groups of interest (Brust et al., 2014; Ren et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work on recombinase-based intersectional methods.

claim: Recombinase-based intersectional methods have been shown to substantially restrict targeting to cell groups of interest.
source: Recombinase-based intersectional methods that combine information about lineage and cell type have been developed in both mice and fruit flies and have been shown to substantially restrict targeting to cell groups of interest (Brust et al., 2014; Ren et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work demonstrating the effectiveness of these methods.

claim: The use of recombinase-based intersectional methods has remained largely limited to specific cases.
source: However, the use of such methods has remained largely limited to specific cases—in mice, sublineages of brainstem serotonergic neurons (Okaty et al., 2015), and in flies, subtypes of Type II transit-amplifying neural stem cells (i.e. neuroblasts, NBs) of the central brain (Ren et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific examples of where these methods have been used.

claim: The limited use of recombinase-based intersectional methods is due to the paucity of lineage-restricted enhancers.
source: This is because of the paucity of lineage-restricted enhancers.
evidence: This is an inference about the reason for the limited use of these methods.

claim: There are few terminal effector gene enhancers that are active in small numbers of mature neurons.
source: Just as there are few TEG enhancers that are active in small numbers of mature neurons
evidence: This is a statement about the availability of specific enhancers, based on knowledge of the field.

claim: There are few identified enhancers that exhibit lineage-specific activity.
source: there are also few identified enhancers that exhibit lineage-specific activity.
evidence: This is a statement about the availability of lineage-specific enhancers, based on knowledge of the field.

claim: A systematic analysis of some 5000 neural enhancer domains identified 761 with activity in embryonic neuroblasts.
source: In the fly, a systematic analysis of some 5000 neural enhancer domains identified 761 with activity in embryonic NBs, but 99 of these expressed in most or all lineages (Manning et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published systematic analysis.

claim: 99 of the 761 neuroblast-active enhancers expressed in most or all lineages.
source: In the fly, a systematic analysis of some 5000 neural enhancer domains identified 761 with activity in embryonic NBs, but 99 of these expressed in most or all lineages (Manning et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published systematic analysis.

claim: The remaining neuroblast-active enhancers are at best active in 5–20 lineages.
source: A separate analysis indicates that the remainder are at best active in 5–20 lineages (Awasaki et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published analysis.

claim: The routine use of lineage-cell type intersections for neural circuit mapping will require more refined methods of isolating neuronal lineages or sub-lineages.
source: The routine use of lineage-cell type intersections for neural circuit mapping will thus require more refined methods of isolating neuronal lineages or sub-lineages.
evidence: This is an inference about what is needed to make lineage-based methods more widely applicable.

claim: The authors introduce a combinatorial method analogous to the Split Gal4 technique to achieve lineage refinement.
source: To achieve such lineage refinement, we introduce here a combinatorial method analogous to the Split Gal4 technique used to restrict neuronal targeting to the intersection of two TEG expression patterns (Luan et al., 2006).
evidence: This describes the approach taken in the manuscript, with a citation to the analogous Split Gal4 technique.

claim: The authors restrict reconstitution of a Split Cre recombinase to the expression patterns of two independent neuroblast-active enhancers.
source: We restrict reconstitution of a Split Cre recombinase to the expression patterns of two independent NB-active enhancers (i.e. NBEs).
evidence: This describes the key mechanism of the SpaRCLIn method.

claim: Only neuroblasts in which both enhancers are active make full-length Cre.
source: Only NBs in which both enhancers are active thus make full-length Cre.
evidence: This describes the specificity of Cre reconstitution in the SpaRCLIn method.

claim: Cre is used to selectively promote activity of the Gal4 transcription factor in the mature progeny of neuroblasts where both enhancers are active.
source: Cre is then used to selectively promote activity of the Gal4 transcription factor—expressed under the control of a TEG enhancer—in the mature progeny of these NBs, thus implementing a second intersection.
evidence: This describes how Cre activity is used to enable Gal4 function in the SpaRCLIn method.

claim: The SpaRCLIn method generalizes the capabilities of the CLIn technique introduced by Ren et al. (2016).
source: Our method (i.e. 'Split Cre-assisted Restriction of Cell Class-Lineage Intersections,' or SpaRCLIn) generalizes the capabilities of the CLIn technique introduced by Ren et al. (2016) by expanding the range of possible intersections to most Drosophila lineages while maintaining compatibility with all existing Drosophila Gal4 driver lines.
evidence: This claim compares SpaRCLIn to the CLIn technique, with a citation to the original CLIn paper.

claim: SpaRCLIn expands the range of possible intersections to most Drosophila lineages.
source: Our method (i.e. 'Split Cre-assisted Restriction of Cell Class-Lineage Intersections,' or SpaRCLIn) generalizes the capabilities of the CLIn technique introduced by Ren et al. (2016) by expanding the range of possible intersections to most Drosophila lineages while maintaining compatibility with all existing Drosophila Gal4 driver lines.
evidence: This describes a key advantage of SpaRCLIn over previous methods.

claim: SpaRCLIn maintains compatibility with all existing Drosophila Gal4 driver lines.
source: Our method (i.e. 'Split Cre-assisted Restriction of Cell Class-Lineage Intersections,' or SpaRCLIn) generalizes the capabilities of the CLIn technique introduced by Ren et al. (2016) by expanding the range of possible intersections to most Drosophila lineages while maintaining compatibility with all existing Drosophila Gal4 driver lines.
evidence: This describes a key advantage of SpaRCLIn in terms of compatibility with existing tools.

claim: The authors have generated two libraries of transgenic fly lines, each expressing distinct Split Cre components under the control of 134 different neuroblast-active enhancers.
source: To facilitate SpaRCLIn's use, we have generated a variety of tools, including two libraries of transgenic fly lines, each of which expresses distinct Split Cre components under the control of 134 different NBEs.
evidence: This describes the reagents generated to implement the SpaRCLIn system.

claim: SpaRCLIn uses a recombinase (Cre) to excise an otherwise ubiquitously expressed construct encoding Gal80.
source: In common with other existing methodologies, SpaRCLIn uses a recombinase (i.e. Cre) to excise an otherwise ubiquitously expressed construct encoding Gal80, a suppressor of the Gal4 transcription factor (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This describes a key mechanism of the SpaRCLIn system, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: Gal80 is a suppressor of the Gal4 transcription factor.
source: In common with other existing methodologies, SpaRCLIn uses a recombinase (i.e. Cre) to excise an otherwise ubiquitously expressed construct encoding Gal80, a suppressor of the Gal4 transcription factor (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is a statement about the function of Gal80, based on established knowledge.

claim: In the SpaRCLIn technique, recombinase expression and excision of Gal80 occurs only in targeted neuroblasts.
source: As in the CLIn technique, recombinase expression—and thus the excision of Gal80—occurs only in targeted NBs, rendering the progeny of these NBs permissive to Gal4 activity (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the specificity of Cre activity in the SpaRCLIn system, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: Excision of Gal80 renders the progeny of targeted neuroblasts permissive to Gal4 activity.
source: As in the CLIn technique, recombinase expression—and thus the excision of Gal80—occurs only in targeted NBs, rendering the progeny of these NBs permissive to Gal4 activity (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the consequence of Gal80 excision in the SpaRCLIn system.

claim: In the SpaRCLIn technique, distinct neuroblast-active enhancers are used to express components of a bipartite Split Cre molecule in restricted subsets of neuroblasts.
source: In the SpaRCLIn technique, distinct NBEs are used to express components of a bipartite Split Cre molecule in restricted subsets of NBs.
evidence: This describes the bipartite version of the SpaRCLIn system.

claim: In lineages of neuroblasts that contain mature neurons within the Gal4 expression pattern, Gal4 will be active.
source: In lineages of these NBs that contain mature neurons within the Gal4 expression pattern, Gal4 will be active.
evidence: This describes the outcome of the SpaRCLIn system when neuroblast lineages overlap with Gal4 expression.

claim: The population of neurons can be additionally parsed using a tripartite Split Cre to further restrict the subset of neuroblasts that make active Cre.
source: This population of neurons can be additionally parsed using a tripartite Split Cre to further restrict the subset of NBs that make active Cre (Figure 1D).
evidence: This describes the tripartite version of the SpaRCLIn system, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: The authors selected Cre for use in SpaRCLIn because of its demonstrated ability to retain high activity in a variety of bipartite forms.
source: Although most recombinase-based expression systems in Drosophila, such as MARCM (Lee and Luo, 1999), Flp-out Gal80 (Gordon and Scott, 2009), and FINGR (Bohm et al., 2010) have preferentially used the Flp recombinase for Gal80 excision, we selected Cre for use in SpaRCLIn because of its demonstrated ability to retain high activity in a variety of bipartite forms (Hirrlinger et al., 2009; Jullien, 2003; Kawano et al., 2016; Kennedy et al., 2010; Rajaee and Ow, 2017).
evidence: This explains the rationale for choosing Cre, supported by citations to published work.

claim: Cre activity has been reported to be toxic in Drosophila when chronically expressed at high levels.
source: Although Cre activity has been reported to be toxic in Drosophila when chronically expressed at high levels (Heidmann and Lehner, 2001; Nern et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published reports of Cre toxicity.

claim: Cre has previously been used in neuroblasts without apparent adverse effects.
source: it has previously been used in NBs without apparent adverse effects (Awasaki et al., 2014; Hampel et al., 2011; Ren et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work using Cre in neuroblasts.

claim: The SpaRCLIn system requires use of a tripartite Cre to achieve the most refined targeting.
source: Because our system requires use of a tripartite Cre to achieve the most refined targeting
evidence: This describes a key feature of the SpaRCLIn system.

claim: It was desirable to use a method of splitting Cre that would permit reconstitution of the intact molecule to obtain the highest activity levels.
source: it was also desirable to use a method of splitting Cre that would permit reconstitution of the intact molecule to obtain the highest activity levels.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the design choice in the SpaRCLIn system.

claim: Split inteins are capable of autocatalytically joining two proteins to which they are fused.
source: Split inteins, which are capable of autocatalytically joining two proteins to which they are fused, are well-suited to this purpose
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of split inteins, based on established knowledge.

claim: Distinct split inteins have been previously shown to support reconstitution of recombinase activity from complementary Cre fragments fused to them.
source: and distinct split inteins have been previously shown to support reconstitution of recombinase activity from complementary Cre fragments fused to them (Ge et al., 2016; Han et al., 2013; Hermann et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work on split inteins and Cre reconstitution.

claim: The breakpoints in Cre separate the amino acid residues that form the DNA-binding sites and the active site.
source: These breakpoints separate the amino acid residues in the primary structure that form the DNA-binding sites (blue) and the active site (yellow highlight), thus insuring that none of the fragments retains catalytic activity.
evidence: This describes the design of the split Cre fragments, with reference to Figure 1E.

claim: The breakpoints in Cre ensure that none of the fragments retains catalytic activity.
source: These breakpoints separate the amino acid residues in the primary structure that form the DNA-binding sites (blue) and the active site (yellow highlight), thus insuring that none of the fragments retains catalytic activity.
evidence: This describes a key design feature of the split Cre system.

claim: Two Split Cre fragments, CreAB and CreC, were generated by the breakpoint between amino acids P250 and S251 to implement the bipartite Split Cre system.
source: Two Split Cre fragments, CreAB and CreC, were generated by the breakpoint between amino acids P250 and S251 to implement the bipartite Split Cre system (Figure 1F,G)
evidence: This describes the design of the bipartite split Cre system, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: Dividing the CreAB fragment at the breakpoint between amino acids D109 and S110 created two further fragments (CreA and CreB) which together with CreC form the basis of the tripartite Split Cre system.
source: while dividing the CreAB fragment at the breakpoint between amino acids D109 and S110 was used to create two further fragments (i.e. CreA and CreB) which together with CreC form the basis of the tripartite Split Cre system (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: This describes the design of the tripartite split Cre system, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: The split intein pairs gp41-1 and NrdJ-1 were chosen based on their trans-splicing efficiency and their lack of cross-reactivity.
source: The split intein pairs used to generate these fragments, gp41-1 and NrdJ-1, were chosen based on their trans-splicing efficiency and their lack of cross-reactivity (Carvajal-Vallejos et al., 2012).
evidence: This explains the rationale for choosing these specific split inteins, with a citation.

claim: The lack of cross-reactivity between split inteins was critical for avoiding the generation of unproductive fusion products of the Cre fragments.
source: The latter criterion was critical for avoiding the generation of unproductive fusion products of the Cre fragments.
evidence: This explains the importance of the lack of cross-reactivity in the design of the system.

claim: The bi- and tripartite constructs were confirmed to reconstitute Cre activity when co-expressed in transfected S2 cells.
source: After confirming the ability of the bi- and tripartite constructs to reconstitute Cre activity when co-expressed in transfected S2 cells (data not shown)
evidence: This describes validation of the split Cre constructs in cell culture.

claim: The authors used the bi- and tripartite constructs to generate transgenic fly lines in which they were expressed in patterns dictated by individual enhancers that exhibited activity in neuroblasts.
source: we used them to generate transgenic fly lines in which they were expressed in patterns dictated by individual enhancers that exhibited activity in neuroblasts.
evidence: This describes the generation of transgenic fly lines for the SpaRCLIn system.

claim: Most of the neuroblast-active enhancers selected were taken from the large collection of enhancer fragments with fully defined sequences created by the Rubin lab.
source: Most of the NBEs selected for this purpose were taken from the large collection of enhancer fragments with fully defined sequences created by the Rubin lab (Pfeiffer et al., 2008 #43).
evidence: This describes the source of most of the enhancers used, with a citation.

claim: Most of the neuroblast-active enhancers selected were from a previously characterized collection of embryonically active neuroblast enhancers.
source: Most of the NBEs selected were from a previously characterized collection of embryonically active NB enhancers (Manning et al., 2012)
evidence: This describes the source of most of the enhancers used, with a citation.

claim: A total of 134 neuroblast-active enhancers were used to make two libraries of transgenic fly lines.
source: A total of 134 NBEs were used to make two libraries of transgenic fly lines, one expressing the CreB fragment under the control of each of the 134 NBEs and the other similarly expressing the CreC fragment.
evidence: This describes the scale of the reagent generation for the SpaRCLIn system.

claim: The two libraries of transgenic fly lines collectively express CreB and CreC in a large number of distinct and often overlapping subsets of neuroblasts.
source: These lines thus collectively express CreB and CreC in a large number of distinct and often overlapping subsets of NBs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the expression patterns of the CreB and CreC libraries, with reference to a figure supplement.

claim: The 134 enhancers are typically active in mature neurons as well as neuroblasts.
source: However, because the 134 enhancers are also typically active in mature neurons, the production of full-length Cre is not necessarily restricted to NBs (Jenett et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes a potential limitation of using these enhancers, with a citation.

claim: To ensure neuroblast-specific reconstitution of Cre activity, the authors placed the CreA and CreAB fragments under the control of a compound enhancer formed by fusing individual enhancer elements of the neuroblast-specific genes deadpan and nerfin-1.
source: To ensure NB-specific reconstitution of Cre activity, we placed the CreA and CreAB fragments under the control of a compound enhancer formed by fusing individual enhancer elements of the NB-specific genes, deadpan (dpn) and nervous fingers-1 (nerfin-1; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the strategy used to ensure neuroblast-specific Cre reconstitution.

claim: The synthetic dpn-nerfin-1 enhancer (DNE) combines the complementary temporal characteristics of both component enhancers.
source: This synthetic dpn-nerfin-1 enhancer (i.e. DNE) combines the complementary temporal characteristics of both component enhancers, maintaining strong, broad, and specific activity throughout embryonic neurogenesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This describes the properties of the DNE, with reference to a figure supplement.

claim: Use of the DNE ensures that full-length, active Cre is generated only in neuroblasts where expression of the Cre fragments overlaps, and not in fully-differentiated neurons.
source: Use of the DNE thus ensured that full-length, active Cre would be generated only in NBs where expression of the Cre fragments overlapped, and not in fully-differentiated neurons (Figure 1G,I).
evidence: This describes the function of the DNE in ensuring neuroblast-specific Cre activity.

claim: The DNE expresses in most of the neuroblasts that give rise to the Drosophila CNS with the exception of those found in the late-developing optic lobes.
source: This enhancer also expresses in most of the NBs that give rise to the Drosophila CNS with the exception of those found in the late-developing optic lobes
evidence: This describes the breadth of DNE expression in neuroblasts.

claim: The DNE guarantees substantial coverage of the mature neurons found within the expression patterns of Gal4 lines.
source: and thus guarantees substantial coverage of the mature neurons found within the expression patterns of Gal4 lines.
evidence: This is an inference about the consequence of broad DNE expression for the utility of the SpaRCLIn system.

claim: The authors created transgenic flies carrying a reporter construct (Cre80Tom) in which the floxed Gal80 gene is followed by the gene encoding tdTomato.
source: To detect activity of the Split Cre constructs in vivo, we created transgenic flies carrying a reporter construct in which the floxed Gal80 gene, the expression of which is driven by a ubiquitously active Actin 5C promoter, is followed by the gene encoding the red fluorescent protein, tdTomato (Figure 1J).
evidence: This describes the reporter construct used to detect Cre activity, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: Expression of tdTomato from the Cre80Tom construct identifies neurons in which Gal80 has been excised.
source: Expression of tdTomato from this construct, which we call Cre80Tom, thus identifies neurons in which Gal80 has been excised.
evidence: This describes the function of the Cre80Tom reporter.

claim: Gal80 excision, identified by the appearance of tdTomato expression, is identifiable as early as embryonic stage eight when the CreAB and CreC fragments are driven by the DNE.
source: Gal80 excision, identified by the appearance of tdTomato expression, is identifiable as early as embryonic stage eight when the CreAB and CreC fragments are driven by the DNE and it is widespread in the developing CNS by stage 13 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This describes the timing of Cre activity in the SpaRCLIn system, with reference to a figure supplement.

claim: The onset of Cre activity is sufficiently early to label many of the progeny of a defined neuroblast lineage targetable by the R59E09-Gal4 line.
source: The onset of Cre activity is sufficiently early to label many of the progeny of a defined NB lineage targetable by the R59E09-Gal4 line, previously identified by Lacin and Truman (2016) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This describes the effectiveness of early Cre activity in labeling neuroblast lineages, with a citation and reference to a figure supplement.

claim: The data suggest that Gal80 excision occurs relatively early.
source: These data suggest that Gal80 excision occurs relatively early.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the timing data on Cre activity.

claim: The bipartite system, using the DNE-CreAB and CreC fragments expressed under the control of two different neuroblast enhancers, generated expression patterns in neuronal lineages of third instar larvae.
source: The bipartite system, using the DNE-CreAB and CreC fragments expressed under the control of two different neuroblast enhancers (NBE43H02 and NBE44F03), also generated expression patterns in neuronal lineages of third instar larvae (Figure 1K and L).
evidence: This describes the application of the bipartite system in larvae, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: The expression patterns generated by the bipartite system include not only the neuroblasts in which Cre activity is reconstituted, but also the progeny of these neuroblasts.
source: The expression patterns include not only the NBs in which Cre activity is reconstituted, but also the progeny of these NBs, since tdTomato expression is activated in all cells born within these lineages after Gal80 is excised.
evidence: This describes the nature of the expression patterns generated by the SpaRCLIn system.

claim: The expression patterns generated by two different neuroblast enhancers in the bipartite system share a small number of common neuroblast lineages.
source: Although the expression patterns differ in the two cases, they share a small number of common NB lineages as is revealed by application of the tripartite Cre system using the NBE44F03 and NBE43H02 enhancers to drive CreB and CreC, respectively, together with DNE-CreA (Figure 1M).
evidence: This describes the overlap between two bipartite expression patterns, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: The tripartite Cre system using NBE44F03 and NBE43H02 enhancers limits expression to approximately three bilateral lineages in the ventral nerve cord and two in the brain.
source: Expression in this case is limited to approximately three bilateral lineages in the ventral nerve cord (VNC) and two in the brain.
evidence: This describes the specificity achieved with the tripartite system, with reference to Figure 1M.

claim: The bi- and tripartite Split Cre constructs selectively reconstitute Cre activity in neuroblasts targeted by individual neuroblast-active enhancers.
source: These examples illustrate how the bi- and tripartite Split Cre constructs selectively reconstitute Cre activity in NBs targeted by individual NBEs
evidence: This is a summary statement about the function of the split Cre constructs.

claim: The tripartite Split Cre system can be used to restrict Cre activity to only those neuroblasts in which two distinct neuroblast-active enhancers are active.
source: and demonstrate that the tripartite Split Cre system can be used to restrict Cre activity to only those NBs in which two distinct NBEs are active.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the capability of the tripartite system.

claim: The tripartite system generates intersections of two NBE-CreC expression patterns by substituting one CreC fragment with a CreB fragment driven by the identical neuroblast-active enhancer.
source: As this example illustrates, the tripartite system generates intersections of two NBE-CreC expression patterns by substituting one CreC fragment with a CreB fragment driven by the identical NBE.
evidence: This describes the strategy for implementing the tripartite system.

claim: All NBE-CreC insertions were made on Chromosome III and all NBE-CreB insertions were made on Chromosome II to facilitate substitutions.
source: To facilitate such substitutions, all NBE-CreC insertions were made on Chromosome III and all NBE-CreB insertions were made on Chromosome II.
evidence: This describes a design feature of the reagent libraries to facilitate their use.

claim: The authors examined NBE-CreC∩DNE-CreAB >CreTom crosses for all 134 neuroblast-active enhancers in multiple preparations to evaluate the reproducibility of expression.
source: To evaluate the reproducibility of expression driven by individual NBEs, we examined NBE-CreC∩DNE-CreAB >CreTom crosses for all 134 NBEs in multiple preparations (on average four per NBE) and compared these patterns with expression observed in all NBE-CreB∩DNE-CreA∩ DNE-CreC >CreTom crosses.
evidence: This describes the evaluation of the reproducibility of the SpaRCLIn system.

claim: In general, the expression patterns were similar across preparations for any given cross.
source: The large size of the patterns and the inability to reliably identify identical neurons and lineages across preparations prevented a systematic analysis, but in general the patterns were similar across preparations for any given cross (Figure 1—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This describes the general reproducibility of expression patterns, with reference to a figure supplement.

claim: In most cases, patterns obtained with a given NBE-CreB line resembled the pattern obtained with the NBE-CreC line made with the same enhancer.
